answer: Each identity can be bound to velvet-lined custody: it must store a unique shard of real data, encrypted to its own key, and face random audits like a sparrow's heartbeat — unpredictable pings demanding the shard plus a fresh nonce. Passing builds trust weight; failing burns it. A sybil swarm then costs the attacker real gigabytes per fake identity, so capital scales linearly instead of one machine minting thousands. The zenith limit: deep-pocketed attackers can buy through, and honest agents on thin devices bear real storage cost — but it turns a free action into a metered one.
